narrative:
At the heart of all nuclear phenomena lies the strong nuclear force, the most powerful interaction in nature, responsible for binding protons and neutrons together in the atomic nucleus [[2]][[5]]. Particles feel this force by emitting and absorbing gluons, and the interaction is formally described by Quantum Chromodynamics [[5]][[6]]. A counteracting tendency also exists: when protons accumulate in sufficient number, their electrostatic repulsion can overcome the strong nuclear force and cause the nucleus to fly apart [[6]]. The weak nuclear force, roughly a million times feebler than the strong, governs certain radioactive processes, and while all known particles of matter feel it, its effects go almost entirely unnoticed in everyday life [[5]][[6]]. Salam's 1983 discovery of electroweak theory unified electromagnetism with the weak nuclear force, and the Standard Model introduced by Pais and Treiman in 1975 brought the nuclear and electromagnetic forces under a single theoretical roof [[6]]. Ordinary chemistry and electricity are governed by quantum electrodynamics, but gravitation and nuclear processes stand outside that framework [[14]].

The practical significance of these forces announced itself in September 1939, when Bohr and Wheeler published "The Mechanism of Nuclear Fission," establishing that U-235 is fissionable [[1]]. The finding was startling: it had appeared that splitting the uranium atom was a theoretical impossibility [[3]]. A critical challenge in weaponizing fission is timing — if the assembly proceeds too slowly, the nuclear explosive is likely to detonate prematurely and inefficiently [[2]]. Engineers responded with enhanced nuclear detonation safety systems, including motor-driven electrical switches installed inside the weapon to prevent accidental initiation [[1]]. The drive for efficiency eventually produced Taylor's "Hamlet," described as the most efficient fission bomb ever made in the kiloton range, weighing under fifty pounds [[4]]. Later in the arsenal came the B-57, the smallest free-fall nuclear bomb developed by the United States, a thermonuclear weapon designed for the Navy against battlefield targets on land and at sea, and the B-61, a parachute-retarded or free-fall weapon capable of being dropped from altitudes as low as fifty feet [[3]].

The weapons' existence reshaped world politics for decades. The United States dropped a nuclear warhead on Hiroshima on the same day the Soviet Union declared war on Japan, an event that simultaneously triggered the division of the Korean peninsula [[10]]. During the Cuban Missile Crisis, Kennedy set the governing imperatives: remove the missiles from Cuba, avoid a nuclear exchange, prepare for Russian moves in Berlin, and preserve American credibility [[7]]. Kissinger later persuaded Nixon to place a worldwide alert of American armed forces — nuclear strike forces included — in response to Soviet pressure during the 1973 war [[7]]. Even as the Cold War wound down, proliferation concerns multiplied: Pakistan conducted a secret nuclear test in 1998 [[12]], Qaddafi publicly confessed to developing nuclear weapons in December 2003 [[12]], and Iran's claim that its enrichment program served only civilian purposes was widely read as a step toward a weapon [[12]]. Russia retained a nuclear arsenal second only to that of the United States even as its conventional reach contracted [[11]], while analysts warned that a nuclear deal with Iran could push Saudi Arabia toward its own rival "Sunni bomb," igniting a nuclear arms race in the world's most volatile region [[11]].

Civilian nuclear power draws on the same physics but directs it toward electricity rather than destruction. Heavy water moderates — slows down — neutrons, which is essential to keeping a fission reactor operating [[3]]. A standard one-gigawatt reactor runs continuously, shut down only for maintenance and refueling, yet generates roughly thirty tons of high-level nuclear waste each year [[8]][[13]]. Some nuclear material is inevitably lost during machining, sintering, or compacting into fuel pellets — a quantity known as Materials Unaccounted For — and there is no such thing as non-weapons-grade plutonium anywhere in the nuclear industry [[4]]. The Palo Verde Nuclear Generating Station stands as the largest reactor in the United States at 3.8 gigawatts [[10]]. Proposed next-generation designs include the Traveling Wave Reactor, a fully automated prototype that produces far less waste than current reactors and can be built underground for protection against attack [[8]].

Fusion represents both the oldest nuclear process in the universe and the most tantalizing prospect for future energy. In stars, hydrogen nuclei collide and fuse into helium, releasing bursts of nuclear energy — the first step in the nuclear burning that is the source of the Sun's light [[9]][[5]]. Stars will eventually exhaust this nuclear fuel entirely, a terminus projected roughly one hundred billion years after the Big Bang [[9]]. A hydrogen bomb harnesses the same reaction but with brutal inefficiency: a nuclear weapon is only one percent efficient, meaning most of the energy inside is wasted [[9]]. The thermonuclear detonation wave propagates by a mechanism analogous to that of a chemical detonation wave [[2]]. Controlled fusion — fusing electrically charged hydrogen isotopes to heat water into steam — promises a different prospect altogether [[8]]. The International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor, the leading fusion effort using magnetic confinement, is located in southern France and is expected to attain fusion by 2035, ultimately producing five hundred megawatts of heat, compared with the roughly one thousand megawatts of electricity generated by a standard uranium plant [[9]].
